title: 3 SGX Next 50 Stocks More than Doubling the STI’s Return YTD
article:
The Straits Times Index lost ground in October, but the dip barely dented a good year.
The
SPDR Straits Times Index ETF
(SGX: ES3), which tracks the
Straits Times Index
(SGX: ^STI), delivered a total return of 18.7% from the start of 2026 to the end of October.
Three SGX
Next 50
stocks did far better.
UMS Integration Limited
(SGX: 558) returned 77.4%.
Frencken Group Limited
(SGX: E28) and
Pan-United Corporation Ltd
(SGX: P52) followed with 43.0% and 40.3%.
These figures include
dividends
, and each one more than doubled the ETF’s gain.
So, did the businesses keep pace with their share prices? It depends on the company.
Is Singapore’s building pipeline showing up in Pan-United’s numbers?
Pan-United is Singapore’s largest ready-mix concrete supplier.
In the first half of 2026 (1H2026), revenue grew 37% year on year (YoY) to S$549.6 million as construction activity picked up across Singapore, Malaysia and Vietnam.
Singapore brought in S$485.9 million, or about 88% of group revenue.
Profit grew even faster.
Net profit attributable to shareholders rose 49% YoY to S$30.6 million.
Operating leverage helped, as did efficiencies from the group’s AiR Digital platform.
Pan-United raised its interim dividend by 50% to S$0.015 per share and paid it on 4 September 2026.
Free cash flow (FCF) improved to S$7.5 million from S$1.0 million a year ago as capital expenditure fell.
The group held S$86.2 million in cash against S$21.0 million in borrowings and S$39.5 million in lease liabilities.
Investors may also be looking ahead.
The Building and Construction Authority (BCA) expects S$47 billion to S$53 billion in construction demand for 2026, and S$31 billion of that had been awarded by June.
Changi Airport Terminal 5, the Marina Bay Sands expansion and MRT extensions anchor the pipeline.
On the flip side, FCF is still thin next to profit.
Trade receivables tied up S$26.0 million as sales grew.
Management also flagged energy costs and supply chain disruptions as risks.
How much of UMS’s profit growth came from its operations?
UMS makes precision parts and assembles equipment modules for
semiconductor
equipment makers.
In the third quarter of 2026 (3Q2026), revenue rose 61% YoY to S$95.4 million, while net profit attributable to shareholders more than doubled to S$21.1 million.
Semiconductor revenue grew 65% to S$83.1 million and aerospace revenue rose 55% to S$9.7 million, as component production ramped up for a new major customer.
Not all of it was good news.
Gross material margin narrowed to 52% from 58.2% because of product mix.
Profit also got a lift from a S$1.6 million foreign exchange gain, which came from currencies, not customers.
Cash flow is more reassuring.
FCF was S$14.9 million, against an outflow of S$10.8 million a year ago.
UMS ended September with S$49.0 million in cash and S$5.0 million in bank borrowings, before completing a S$138.6 million share placement in October.
The board proposed a third interim dividend of S$0.010 per share, payable on 18 December 2026.
With 177.6 million bonus shares issued in January and 52.9 million placement shares in October, that rate now applies to more shares.
What might investors be paying for?
Possibly what comes next.
UMS’s new major customer has issued upbeat guidance on AI-driven demand.
Industry association SEMI expects global spending on 300mm chip fabrication equipment to rise 31% to US$149 billion in 2026.
Why did Frencken’s shares rise when its profit fell?
Frencken builds complex electro-mechanical assemblies and plastic components for semiconductor, healthcare and automotive companies, among others.
At first glance, its 1H2026 results looked flat: revenue slipped 0.8% YoY to S$427.8 million and net profit attributable to shareholders fell 3.4% to S$19.3 million.
The detail looks better.
Gross margin widened by 0.9 percentage points to 15.0%, and gross profit grew 5.8% to S$64.4 million.
Administrative expenses rose 9.9% on staff and transformation costs.
Management expects 2H2026 revenue to beat both 2H2025 and 1H2026.
It guides for higher full-year revenue and profit, with semiconductor sales expected to rise.
To put it simply, investors may be paying for where Frencken is heading, not where it has been.
Cash flow is the part to watch.
FCF swung to an outflow of S$15.3 million from an inflow of S$50.6 million a year ago, as inventories and receivables absorbed S$81.6 million.
Frencken still holds S$68.8 million in net cash.
The missing interim dividend is normal, as Frencken pays dividends once a year with its full-year results.
FCF is the lifeblood of dividends, so second-half cash flow will shape the final payout.
Get Smart: Write down what the price expects
All three share one trait.
Their share prices appear to reflect where earnings could go, not just where they are today.
A simple habit helps here.
When a stock runs ahead of its results, write down what the business needs to deliver next.
For Frencken, that means a stronger second half and higher full-year profit.
For UMS, it means sales from its new major customer growing without margins slipping further.
Then check each set of results against your list, and you will know quickly whether the story still holds.

title: US logs US$404 billion deficit in first month of fiscal year
article:
(Nov 13) : The US budget gap widened to US$404 billion in October, up 42% from the same period a year earlier, Treasury Department data showed Thursday.

In the first month of the fiscal year that began Oct. 1, government spending rose 12%, to US$773 billion, and tax receipts declined by 9%, to US$369 billion.

Higher spending on the military, healthcare and interest on the debt pushed up government outlays last month. Bigger tariff and corporate tax refunds weighed on tax receipts, though tariff refunds have slowed since the summer. Overall, tariff revenue dropped roughly 39% from October 2025, to US$19.2 billion.

The Treasury estimated the US budget gap will widen slightly this year to roughly US$2.2 trillion, the report showed.

The government recorded a US$1.99 trillion shortfall in the last fiscal year, as spending far outpaced federal tax collection and rising interest rates sent government debt costs soaring. That pushed the annual deficit to roughly 6% of gross domestic product.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has said he wants to bring the annual US deficit down to 3% of GDP but hasn’t proposed specific plans for cutting spending or boosting revenues, except through higher tariffs. Bessent has said that if the US continued growing at the same pace as the third quarter of 2026, the federal government could grow its way out of the current deficit.

See also: Stocks fall on Nvidia rout as oil jump sinks bonds

Most economists have dismissed that argument, saying the US would need more than 8% sustained economic growth to meaningfully decrease the deficit. President Donald Trump has also floated large spending increases, including calling for a US$350 billion bump in defense spending.

On tariffs, the Treasury projected that the US would bring in US$464 billion custom duties this fiscal year, an estimate that exceeds the current pace of collection under existing tariffs.

See also: Nvidia board members tap Wachtell’s Kim for Huang probe

Last year, the department collected less than half of the US$404 billion it projected in tariff revenue, after the Supreme Court in February overturned a large swath of Trump’s tariffs, forcing the administration to refund roughly US$166 billion of so-called IEEPA duties to importers.

As of Nov. 5, Customs and Border Protection has sent approximately US$128.4 billion in refund payments — which include interest — to Treasury for disbursement, according to a court filing.

After the Supreme Court ruling, Trump vowed to restore tariff revenue and quickly put in place temporary global tariffs while his administration prepared more durable duties under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974.

A new set of tariffs linked to forced labor came into force on goods from more than 60 economies over the summer, just as the temporary duties expired. Trump also recently imposed duties on billions worth of goods imported from Canada under a never-before used tariff authority.

The administration is also expected to roll out another set of Section 301 duties on imports from several major trading partners related to excess industrial capacity in the next few months.

title: Stocks fall on Nvidia rout as oil jump sinks bonds
article:
(Nov 13) : A leadership crisis at Nvidia Corp. curbed the appetite for riskier corners on Wall Street, with stocks also declining as a rally in oil prices lifted Treasury yields.

The company at the heart of the AI boom sank 4.3% as Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang was ousted. The US is probing Alice Huang, the woman officials suspect as a possible spy, over whether entities linked to her were involved in efforts to smuggle Super Micro Computer Inc.’s products to China. Anthropic PBC’s IPO was said to be about six times oversubscribed.

Most S&P 500 firms fell. Also weighing on sentiment was an increase in energy costs. President Donald Trump said the US doesn’t need a deal with Iran and instructed Vice President JD Vance to focus on domestic issues. Bond yields rose on bets the Federal Reserve will step up the pace of rate hikes to cool inflation.

While Nvidia’s board hunts for someone to permanently replace Huang, it’s counting on Colette Kress — the company’s chief financial officer of 13 years and a longtime technology executive — to steady the ship as interim CEO.

“When a star leaves a Wall Street firm, the first question is always the same: Did the clients sign with the banker or with the bank?” said Mark Malek at Siebert Financial. “Nvidia is about to answer that question on the biggest stage in the market.”

As for the broader artificial-intelligence trade, Malek notes that the biggest buyers are funding the buildout out of their own cash flow, and “they need the chips no matter whose name is on the door.”

See also: Nvidia board members tap Wachtell’s Kim for Huang probe

“Leadership transitions can be disruptive, especially when the departing executive helped create the company’s success,” said veteran strategist Louis Navellier. “But I don’t believe a shocking headline, by itself, is a reason to abandon a fundamentally strong investment.”

Navellier’s plan is to hold Nvidia through earnings, review the company’s results and guidance, and reassess from there.

“Despite this uncertainty, the corporate fundamentals around the giant chipmaker are unchanged, and it remains to be seen if a shift at the top of the organization will have a material effect on strategy and execution going forward,” said James McCann at Edward Jones.

See also: OpenAI third quarter revenue soars nearly 50% to US$10 billion

Other companies may look to capitalize on the uncertainty, but the leadership questions do not erase Nvidia’s position as a best-in-class technology company, according to Bret Kenwell at eToro.

“Nvidia’s earnings already demand close attention, but they will be under an even brighter spotlight next week,” he said. “Investors will be looking to Nvidia for a fresh read on demand and a reason to regain confidence.”

title: US stocks bounce as Nvidia rout spurs gains elsewhere
article:
(Nov 13): A leadership crisis at Nvidia Corp spurred a selloff in its shares, but ended up fuelling a rotation into a broader category of stocks.

The company at the heart of the artificial-intelligence (AI) boom tumbled 5% after chief executive officer Jensen Huang was ousted from his post. The plunge sent its market capitalisation below US$4 trillion. Despite the turmoil, the S&P 500 edged up, with about half of its sectors rising. The list of gainers includes chip giants like Advanced Micro Devices Inc and Broadcom Inc.

While Nvidia’s board hunts for someone to permanently replace Huang, it’s counting on Colette Kress — the company’s chief financial officer of 13 years and a longtime technology executive — to steady the ship as interim CEO.

“In the near term, investors should expect significant volatility in Nvidia,” said Ken Mahoney at Mahoney Asset Management. “Longer term, we believe this could ultimately present an opportunity for investors with the appropriate time horizon.”

Nvidia remains a vitally important company with tremendous earnings power and a central role in the AI revolution, he added.

Elsewhere, oil rose as President Donald Trump said the US doesn’t need a deal with Iran and instructed Vice President JD Vance to focus on domestic issues rather than negotiations with Tehran. Bond yields climbed. Bitcoin sank.

See also: US stocks climb as Wall Street gets fresh AI fuel
• Chinese AI stocks fell on concerns that cloud operators’ access to advanced chips may face tighter US scrutiny amid the escalating espionage and leadership controversy surrounding Nvidia.
• Nebius Group NV sank after the AI computing provider reported a disappointing sales outlook and backer Nvidia ousted its CEO.
• Alphabet Inc raised almost US$4 billion-equivalent of funds in Asia through inaugural Hong Kong- and Singapore-dollar bond sales, testing investor appetite at a time of increasing volatility for companies focused on AI.
• Strategy Inc fell after MSCI Inc dropped the Bitcoin accumulator from its global equity benchmarks, potentially triggering billions of dollars in stock sales.

title: Nvidia market cap sinks below US$4 tril following Huang's resignation
article:
(Nov 13): Nvidia Corp’s stock plunged at the open on Thursday, taking the chipmaker’s market capitalisation below US$4 trillion for the first time since 2025, after chief executive officer Jensen Huang resigned following the revelation of two affairs, one with a suspected Chinese spy.

The shares were down as much as 14% in early trading, dropping to their lowest since June 2025, erasing as much as US$601 billion in market value. If that holds through the close, it will be the largest one-day market capitalisation wipeout for any stock ever.

The stock has shed roughly 35% from a record hit in early October, cutting its market value by US$2 trillion in a matter of week. Nvidia was the biggest company in the world just a few weeks ago, but at less than US$3.8 trillion it’s currently below Apple Inc and Microsoft Corp.

“I’ve never seen something quite like this, so we’re in new territory,” said Ted Mortonson, technology strategist at Robert W Baird & Co. “On a scale of one to 10, this is a 10.”

Huang’s ability to stay at the helm of the most important artificial intelligence (AI) chipmaker has been under scrutiny since Sunday, when he admitted to a romantic relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at the Singaporean data centre firm Megaspeed International who’s suspected of spying for China. Then on Wednesday, the New York Times reported that Huang also had a relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare, citing unidentified people who worked at the company.

See also: Nvidia’s Jensen Huang resigns; CFO Colette Kress to serve as interim CEO

Nvidia announced Huang’s departure before the market opened on Thursday, naming chief financial officer Colette Kress interim CEO and board member Harvey Jones as its first-ever chairman.

The news comes ahead of Nvidia’s third-quarter earnings report next Tuesday. The company expected to show strong growth amid robust demand for AI chips, but the scandals are causing investors and analysts to flee the stock, with at least seven Wall Street firms downgrading Nvidia over the past week. Meanwhile, the cost of protecting the firm’s debt against default neared a record.

The questions surrounding Huang added to growing concerns about the strength and longevity of the AI trade overall. Quarterly results from major Nvidia customers like Alphabet Inc, Amazon.com Inc and Meta Platforms Inc underscored how investors are losing patience with big spending on AI, especially as it turns cash flows negative.

See also: Alibaba shares drop 7% as Nvidia saga triggers chip access fears

At the same time, the US midterm elections showed many voters oppose building data centres anywhere near their communities, further clouding the outlook for spending, which translates to revenue at chipmakers and other companies involved in AI infrastructure.

Nvidia is down 15% in 2026, on track for its worst year since 2022. In contrast, the Philadelphia Stock Exchange Semiconductor Index is up 47% this year.
